title: Dawn, awake
hookLine: the morning star rises; he is the Buddha, the one who woke up

cards: Before a sunrise, there's a stretch when the sky goes from dark to not-dark, and nobody watching can say exactly when it happened.
On a camping trip, after a sleepless night, from the window of an early flight, it looks the same.

Some mornings, low in the east, one bright point of light hangs on after the other stars have faded: the morning star, the planet Venus. The wanderer has sat through the whole night. The third watch is ending.
And the tellings, especially in East Asia, say that as the morning star rose, it was done. Today's word is what he had become.

teach.h: BUDDHA — THE ONE WHO WOKE UP.
teach.b: Buddha isn't a name. It's a description, from the same root as bodhi: budh, to wake up. Buddha means the one who has woken up, the awakened one.
The man under the tree was Siddhattha Gotama, a Sakyan, a former prince, a wanderer. At dawn, Buddhists say, he became the Buddha.
The suttas tell a story about this very word. Some time later, a brahmin named Dona sees the Buddha's footprints on a road, marked with wheels, and follows them, amazed.
He finds him sitting under a tree and asks: are you a god? No, says the Buddha. A heavenly musician?
A human being? No. Then what are you?

Everything that would make him any of those, the Buddha explains, has been cut off at the root, like a palm tree stump that can't grow again. Like a lotus that grows in the water and rises above it, unsoiled.
So remember me, he says, as awake. Traditions remember the day differently.
Theravada Buddhists celebrate the awakening on Vesak, a full-moon day that also remembers his birth and his death.

In Japan, the day of awakening is kept in December, and some Zen monasteries sit through the night before it, waiting for the morning star. Different calendars, the same dawn, and the same one word. Not a god.

how: Theravada Buddhists celebrate the awakening on Vesak, the full moon of the month of Vesakha, and in Japan it is kept as Bodhi Day (Rohatsu) in December, in some Zen communities with meditation through the night.

o: the one who has woken up
a god who came down to earth

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: it's a description: the awakened one. his name was Siddhattha Gotama.
asked if he was a god, the Buddha said no
not a god, a spirit or a heavenly musician. remember me as awake.
every Buddhist tradition celebrates the awakening on the same day
Theravada Buddhists keep it on Vesak; in Japan it's kept in December.

games.q: you're Dona. you follow extraordinary footprints to a man under a tree. you ask: are you a god? a spirit? a human? what does he say?
o: I am a human, like you.
games.why: he says no to each, and then: remember me as awake. Buddha. like a lotus risen above the water, unsoiled by it.

practice: If there's a window, face toward the light; if not, close your eyes and picture a sunrise: the dark sky, a thin line of light in the east, one bright star still hanging there.
Watch the sky change slowly, from black to deep blue to gray to gold, without hurrying it. As the light comes, notice your own awareness, the simple fact that you are awake, right now, seeing.

wordCard.voice: Buddha. The awakened one, the one who woke up, from the root budh. Not a name, but what Siddhattha became at dawn.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakened, the one who has woken up; from budh, to wake.

carryVoice: Your line: awake. One word, and it was what he had become. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dona Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 4.36): remember me as awake
